title: Frequently asked questions (FAQ)
intro: Short, clear answers to the most frequently asked questions — each answer links to the topic where the material is covered in depth.
keyPoints: Sixteen short answers, grouped by theme: basics → learning → choosing → judging.
Each answer fits in a few sentences; the link below it points to the full topic.
Use the search bar (shortcut /) to jump straight to a concept.

blocks.html:
What is the difference between classification and regression?

Classification predicts a category (spam or not), regression a continuous number (a price). In scikit-learn: .predict() returns labels versus numbers. Note: despite its name, logistic regression is a classifier. See Supervised learning.

Why is it called logistic "regression" if it classifies?

The name refers to the log-odds being linearly regressed on the features; the output is a probability clipped into a class at threshold 0.5. See Logistic regression.

Supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement learning?

Supervised learns from examples with answers (X and y); unsupervised finds structure without labels (KMeans, PCA); reinforcement learns from rewards. See The three types of machine learning.

What exactly are features, labels, X and y?

Rows are samples, columns are features; the label (target) is the column you predict. X is the 2D feature matrix, y the 1D target vector. Encode categorical columns first (one-hot). See Data, features & labels.

Why must I split train and test data?

A model can memorize its training data; the test set plays “new data” and is used only once, at the end. Split first and fit transformers on the training data only (no leakage). See Data, features & labels.

What is cross-validation and when do I need it?

One split is a gamble; CV repeats the split k times and averages: cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5). Essential for hyperparameter tuning (GridSearchCV), with a Pipeline once preprocessing is involved. See Cross-validation.

How do I build logistic regression myself, without scikit-learn?

Five lines: sigmoid, bias column, zero weights, and per epoch y_hat = sigmoid(Xb @ w), grad = Xb.T @ (y_hat - y) / n, w -= lr * grad. Add predict_proba and predict — done. See Building logistic regression.

What is overfitting and how do I recognize it?

Overfitting = learned the training data too precisely, noise included. Spot the gap: high train, low test score. Countermeasures: simpler model, more data, more regularization (smaller C). See The ML workflow.

How does a model actually ‘learn’?

Two steps: a loss function measures how wrong the model is; gradient descent nudges the weights one step downhill. Repeat until the loss barely moves; the learning rate sets the step size. See Loss functions and Gradient descent.

What does regularization do and what does C mean?

Regularization adds a penalty for large coefficients (against overfitting). C is the inverse strength: large C = little penalty, small C = a lot. Too far down → underfitting. See Regularization.

What exactly are bias and variance?

Bias = systematic error (underfitting: poor on train and test); variance = jitter (overfitting: perfect train, poor test). Expected error = bias² + variance + noise. See Bias-variance tradeoff.

How much math do I need for machine learning?

Starting takes almost none; understanding runs on three pillars: derivatives, optimization and a little probability. The Calculus & optimization chapter covers the first two from scratch.

LogisticRegression or an SVM?

Both linear classifiers; the difference is the loss. LR naturally gives probabilities (predict_proba); SVMs maximize the margin and learn non-linear boundaries with kernels. Scale your features and let the test data decide. See LR vs. SVM.

What does a kernel do in an SVM?

A kernel computes similarity as if the samples live in a higher dimension (the kernel trick) — non-linear boundaries with linear math. Start linear, switch to RBF only if the data is not separable. See Kernel SVMs.

Why should I scale my features?

KNN, SVMs and gradient methods are scale-sensitive: one feature in the thousands dominates everything. StandardScaler sets columns to mean 0, spread 1 — fit on the training data. Trees are insensitive. See Data, features & labels.

When do I choose a decision tree over a linear model?

Tree when explainability matters or the data naturally jumps in thresholds (no scaling needed); linear model for a smooth, linear pattern. A single tree is jittery — see Bias-variance tradeoff.

Should I pick Gini or entropy for my decision tree?

Almost never a real choice: strongly correlated (Gini ≤ H/2) and the same splits. Gini is the cheap default (CART); entropy belongs to ID3/C4.5 and measures in bits. See Gini index & entropy.

What is the difference between bagging and boosting?

Bagging (random forest): parallel on bootstrap sets, averages — mainly lowers variance. Boosting (gradient boosting, XGBoost): sequential, each model learns from its predecessor's errors — mainly lowers bias. Forest = friendly default; boosting for the last bit of performance. See Bagging & random forests.

What does predict_proba do and when do I need probabilities?

.predict() gives hard labels; .predict_proba() per-class probabilities (summing to 1). Useful with asymmetric error costs: pick your own threshold (e.g. “treat above 0.3”) to tune precision and recall. See Probabilities & the sigmoid.

My accuracy is 95% — is my model good?

Not necessarily: with 95 healthy and 5 sick patients, “always healthy” also scores 95% while finding zero sick ones. Precision, recall and F1 give the honest picture. Run the example below yourself.

blocks.caption: accuracy can mislead — four metrics with skewed classes
blocks.source:
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score

# 100 patients: 95 healthy (class 0), 5 sick (class 1)
y_test = [0] * 95 + [1] * 5

# the model predicts 'healthy' (class 0) for everyone
y_pred = [0] * 100

print("accuracy :", accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred))
print("precision:", precision_score(y_test, y_pred, zero_division=0))
print("recall   :", recall_score(y_test, y_pred))
print("f1-score :", f1_score(y_test, y_pred, zero_division=0))

blocks.html: In the output: accuracy 0.95, but precision, recall and F1 all 0.0 — the model finds no positive cases at all. See Classification metrics.

Which metric do I use for regression?

MSE punishes large errors quadratically; RMSE is in your target's unit; MAE is less outlier-sensitive; R² compares against the “always predict the mean” baseline. Big outliers? Look at MAE. See Regression metrics.

Why does my regression tree predict the same price for 200 m² as for 114 m²?

Because a leaf predicts a constant mean and trees cannot extrapolate: outside the training range the tree repeats its highest leaf. Trends beyond the range need linear regression. See Regression trees.
